newsitem.title: UK: Gloom encircles Major before key party conference.
newsitem.headline: Gloom encircles Major before key party conference.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, his pre-election party conference already overshadowed by allegations of sleaze, was accused on Monday of lacking leadership and espousing a futile policy over Europe.

Major was hoping the Conservative conference that opens on Tuesday in the resort of Bournemouth would mark an end to party squabbling and concentrate supporters' attention on beating the Labour opposition in a general election, to be called by May.
But events over the weekend showed theTories, in power since 1979, are in a sorry state.
Allegations of sleaze, an embarrassing defection, poor opinion poll ratings and splits over Europe have added to the gloom cast by Labour's successful conference last week.

Former party treasurer Lord Robert McAlpine -- a wealthy confidant of former premier Margaret Thatcher and a key fund-raiser for her election campaigns -- resigned from the party over the weekend to join the Referendum Party of businessman Sir James Goldsmith.
Goldsmith wants voters to be given the chance to vote in a referendum on Britain's relations with the European Union.

Arguing that a plebiscite should be conducted quickly, McAlpine told BBC radio: "The country needs to know which direction it's going in. We can't say "Oh, we'll leave that'. This is a philosophy of futility."

Major, striving to bridge a yawning gap between so-called Eurosceptics and pro-Europeans like finance minister Kenneth Clarke, has pledged a referendum if, after the election, he decided it was in Britain's interests to join a single currency.
Clarke is likely to be a focus of attention for right-wing Conservatives, who want him to cut taxes to improve the Conservatives election chances, at the conference.
Media reports say Clarke may be booed and claim some delegates may be preparing to demand his resignation.

Former Conservative chairman, Lord Norman Tebbit, slammed Major's wait-and-see attitude to the proposed single European currency, saying he must tell voters before the election whether he would be prepared to abandon the pound sterling.
"You cannot lead from a position of saying "I have not made up my mind'," Tebbit, a right-winger also close Thatcher, said in an interview with the Times.
He told the newspaper a party going into the election without a policy on the issue would be "smoked out" by the electors in the heat of the poll battle.
Major's problems over policy were far from his only headache, as a row over sleaze within the party rumbled on.

Former Conservative minister Neil Hamilton is at the centre of the row after admitting accepting 10,000 pounds ($15,000) from political lobbyist Ian Greer, but denying he took money in return for asking questions in parliament.

Greer announced at the weekend he was resigning as chairman of his lobbying company and immediately gave an interview to the Times in which he said he had raised 750,000 pounds (more than $1 million) for the Conservatives over the past decade.
He also said he was paid to provide a car and offices for the 1990 campaign at which Major won the party leadership and ministers had approached him for help with election expenses.
Opinion polls indicated that Labour unity and Conservative dissension had widened the gap between the two. One in the Sunday Times said Labour's lead increased to 23 points from 19.

Moderate Conservative member of parliament Julian Critchley wrote in the Independent that Major was "facing this week the most difficult party conference...since 1963, and one at which he must make the speech of his life."
At the 1963 conference, senior party figures scrambled for the premiership after Harold MacMillan announced he would have to step down because of ill health.
